questions.q: Per this lesson, what skill is a System Architect-style exam scenario actually testing, as opposed to a simple recall question?
options: Whether the candidate can recall a single isolated fact, such as a feature's name
Whether the candidate can type quickly under time pressure
Whether, given a messy and realistic situation, the candidate can reason to the right combination of concepts and defend the recommendation
Whether the candidate has memorized every governor limit number
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes architecture-level scenarios from junior-level recall questions -- the skill being tested is reasoning through a realistic, ambiguous situation to a justified recommendation, not recalling an isolated fact.

questions.q: In Worked Scenario 1 (the order visibility problem), why does the lesson rule out the nightly batch export option, even though it would satisfy the stated staleness tolerance?
options: Because nightly batch exports are technically impossible to build
Because a batch copy is, by definition, a second copy that can drift from the ERP's own number between refreshes -- which the scenario explicitly rules out
Because the ERP team refused to allow any integration at all
Because batch integrations always violate Salesforce's governor limits
questions.explain: Although batch would satisfy the few-hours-of-staleness tolerance, the scenario explicitly rules out a duplicated, independently-maintained copy that can drift -- which a batch export is by definition, making data virtualization the defensible choice instead.

questions.q: In Worked Scenario 2 (the contractor offboarding gap), what specific gap does the lesson identify as the root cause?
options: The corporate identity provider was never implemented at all
The contractor's SSO credentials were stolen by an external attacker
Salesforce has no concept of user deactivation
Deactivating the identity provider account didn't automatically deactivate the separately-provisioned Salesforce user record, because deprovisioning wasn't synchronized
questions.explain: The lesson identifies the root cause as a deprovisioning gap -- SSO authentication was disabled at the IdP, but the separately-provisioned Salesforce account wasn't automatically deactivated in sync, since no ongoing synchronization mechanism was connecting the two.

questions.q: What does this lesson say makes a recommendation 'defensible' under exam conditions?
options: Stating any generic best practice that happens to also be true, regardless of the scenario's specific details
Naming the specific constraint that rules out the tempting-but-wrong option, naming the fitting concept, and tracing the recommendation back to the scenario's own stated facts
Giving the longest possible answer with the most technical jargon
Avoiding any mention of why an alternative option was rejected
questions.explain: The lesson's defensible-answer structure requires naming the specific ruling-out constraint, the specific fitting concept, and stating a recommendation traceable to the scenario's own facts -- not a generic best practice stated in the abstract.

questions.q: What mechanism does this lesson recommend to fix the contractor offboarding gap in Worked Scenario 2?
options: Switching entirely away from SSO back to separate passwords for every system
Simply asking contractors to self-report when their contract ends
An ongoing synchronization mechanism, such as Identity Connect or SCIM, keeping the Salesforce user record's active/inactive status synchronized with the authoritative HR or directory system
Deleting all contractor accounts preemptively on day one of their contract
questions.explain: The lesson recommends an ongoing sync mechanism (Identity Connect or SCIM, per Lesson 14) that keeps the Salesforce user record's status synchronized with the authoritative system, closing the specific automation gap that caused the stale access.
